item.title: Explaining AI-Image Detection: What the Heatmap Actually Shows
item.description:
Priority: 60/100 (Skim, confidence: high)

Quality dimensions: Author 42, Paper 55, Empirical 88, Reproducibility 30, Manuscript 90

Missing quality signals: Author affiliations or institution metadata, Author citation counts and h-indexes, DOI, journal, or conference acceptance, Paper citation or influential-citation data, Open-source code or repository, Public dataset or data-release statement

Score evidence: Evaluation covers 186,527 images and uses a product-disjoint split.; Controlled re-encoding changes the strongest model from 0.9999 to 0.7254 PR-AUC.; A three-seed factorial attributes +0.176 ± 0.009 PR-AUC to the encoding change.; Five public detectors and 17 attribution methods are evaluated.

TL;DR: The paper shows that AI-generated marketplace-photo detection is heavily confounded by encoding history and proposes causally controlled evaluation of both detectors and attribution maps, finding that strong heatmap performance does not establish faithful explanation.

Problem: Detect forged or AI-generated marketplace review photographs while providing attribution maps as evidence, despite compression and encoding artifacts that can create misleading detection performance and explanations.

Method: The authors evaluate a detector-plus-attribution-map system on 186,527 images using product-disjoint splits, controlled re-encoding, a three-seed factorial experiment, forensic-feature analysis, detector-blind attribution controls, edited and generated image subsets, and comparisons across 17 mapping methods and five public detectors. They select a detector after harmonizing the final encoding of both classes and construct an ensembled regional attribution map.

Key contribution: The genuinely new element is a control-driven framework that treats encoding history as a causal confounder in AI-image detection and tests attribution maps against controls that do not consult the detector. It distinguishes maps that merely localize edits from explanations faithful to the detector, explicitly concluding that the latter was not demonstrated.

Main result: A model scoring 0.9999 PR-AUC on a product-disjoint split fell to 0.7254 after synthetics were re-encoded into the real-image format. Applying one identical final encode to both classes produced a gain attributed entirely to encoding (+0.176 ± 0.009 PR-AUC across three seeds), although forensic features still achieved 0.7145 PR-AUC at a 0.254 base rate. For attribution, 12 of 17 maps beat a detector-blind control on edited images and eight did so on generated images; perturbation methods led both axes, no gradient-CAM variant had positive advantage, and the regional ensemble achieved the best pixel AP in 12.4 seconds per map versus 44.9 seconds for occlusion.

Limitation: The abstract reports no faithful detector explanation: beating detector-blind localization controls is insufficient to show that a heatmap represents the detector's actual reasoning. It also provides no code, public-data, external-domain, statistical-significance, or deployment evidence, and the selected detector's final aggregate performance is not stated clearly in the abstract.

Relevance: The paper directly matches the query "causality" because it uses controlled interventions on image encoding and detector-blind controls to test whether apparent detection and attribution gains are causally connected to synthesis, image edits, or the detector itself.

Tags: causality, AI-image detection, explainable AI, attribution maps, image forensics, compression confounding, marketplace fraud, computer vision

Figure note: A useful image would diagram the controlled pipeline: real and synthetic inputs, asymmetric versus shared final encoding, detector evaluation, attribution methods, detector-blind controls, and the distinction between localization performance and faithful explanation.

Quality dimensions: Author 34, Paper 55, Empirical 58, Reproducibility 72, Manuscript 72

TL;DR: The paper presents a multi-view graph and multi-source unsupervised domain-adaptation framework for cross-site MDD classification from rs-fMRI, reporting 73.60% mean accuracy across seven unlabeled target domains.

Problem: Cross-site MDD identification from rs-fMRI suffers from acquisition-related distribution shifts and heterogeneous functional-connectivity views with different biases and graph structures.

Method: The framework constructs Pearson-correlation, sparse-representation, and Granger-causality graphs; processes them with view-specific graph attention networks; combines pairwise view interactions through dual-stream adaptive fusion; applies hyperbolic residual encoding; and aligns domains using class-wise Cauchy–Schwarz alignment, adversarial learning, information maximization, and confidence-aware pseudo-labeling.

Key contribution: Its claimed novelty is the joint treatment of heterogeneous multi-view connectome learning and multi-source unsupervised domain adaptation, augmented by curvature-aware hyperbolic representation refinement.

Main result: Across seven unlabeled target domains, the method obtains 73.60% mean accuracy and 71.90% AUC. The abstract does not provide baseline results, uncertainty estimates, statistical tests, per-domain performance, or ablations, so the magnitude and robustness of the improvement cannot be assessed.

Limitation: The abstract gives no named datasets, sample sizes, baseline comparisons, ablations, statistical robustness analysis, or external clinical validation. It also does not isolate the contribution of Granger-causality graphs or establish causal inference beyond using Granger-derived connectivity.

Relevance: The paper matches the query “causality” because Granger causality is used to construct one functional-connectivity view. Its central focus, however, is domain adaptation and MDD classification rather than general causal discovery or causal-effect estimation.

item.title: Transcript-Managed Transformers: Monotone Multi-Agent Collapse and Universality with Two Pop-Enabled Transcripts
item.description:

Score evidence: The submission is arXiv v1, dated 2026-07-31, with no DOI or journal reference supplied.; The abstract explicitly states finite-state, deterministic context-free, and recursively enumerable expressivity results.; The scope assumptions explicitly fix precision, alphabets, blocks, visibility, controller state, and population.; The manuscript is described as 14 pages with 2 tables and 0 figures.

TL;DR: The paper gives a formal transducer model of transcript management in fixed-precision causal Transformers, proving that append-only systems remain finite-state while two pop-enabled transcript channels suffice for Turing universality.

Problem: It studies how transcript operations affect the computational power of fixed, finite-precision causal Transformers and finite multi-agent systems when models, weights, token protocols, visible context, and population size remain fixed.

Method: The authors introduce Transcript-Managed Transducers with a finite controller, bounded-block channels, fixed visible suffixes, and stay, push, or pop actions. They relate the pop-free model to deterministic finite-state transductions and compile pop-enabled channels into classical stack-machine formulations to transfer known automata-theoretic results.

Key contribution: The central novelty is a sharp computational boundary for transcript management: monotone append, route, and copy protocols do not lift fixed finite agent populations beyond finite-state computation, whereas exposing a PopContext operation turns channels into stacks, yielding deterministic context-free power with one channel and recursively enumerable power with two or more.

Main result: The abstract claims exact finite-state expressivity for every fixed number of append-only channels and every fixed finite monotone agent population; with pop, one channel realizes deterministic context-free languages and at least two channels realize recursively enumerable computation. It also states that two one-channel agents can match a single two-channel controller.

Limitation: The evidence is theoretical: the abstract reports no experiments, Transformer implementations, benchmark comparisons, ablations, or robustness analysis. Results rely on fixed precision, alphabets, block size, visibility radius, controller state, and agent population, while growing context, hidden-block access, writable storage, or unbounded spawning introduce additional state and fall outside the stated bounds.

Relevance: The match to “causality” is indirect: the paper concerns causal Transformers, meaning autoregressive information flow, rather than causal inference, causal discovery, or treatment-effect estimation. It is potentially useful if the feed targets theoretical properties of causal language-model architectures, but likely peripheral for a causality-focused research feed.

item.title: Evidence-Type Competition: When Can Interventional Data Teach Language Models Causal Direction?
item.description:
Priority: 59/100 (Skim, confidence: medium)

Quality dimensions: Author 40, Paper 58, Empirical 82, Reproducibility 35, Manuscript 88

Missing quality signals: Author affiliation and institution, Author citation count and h-index, DOI, journal, or conference acceptance, Open-source code or repository, Public dataset or synthetic-data generator, Detailed baseline comparisons

Score evidence: arXiv v1, published July 31, 2026; no DOI or journal reference supplied.; The abstract reports controlled experiments across 50 Simpson’s-paradox worlds.; A matched second seed preserved 11/11 strong reversals.; A 0.93B-parameter experiment reports 31.8% versus 6% reversal rates.

TL;DR: In controlled Simpson’s-paradox settings, language models can learn causal effects from interventional pretraining data yet suppress that knowledge when observational evidence appears in the inference context.

Problem: The paper tests whether adding interventional data during pretraining is sufficient to teach language models the correct direction of causal effects when observational correlations point in the opposite direction.

Method: The author constructs controlled synthetic Simpson’s-paradox worlds, varies the proportion of interventional pretraining samples and the evidence type supplied at inference, performs content manipulations and activation patching, tests seed and model-scale robustness, audits behavior on CLadder, and evaluates an evidence-averaging protocol.

Key contribution: The central finding is an evidence-type competition mechanism: causal capability can reside in model weights while observational context suppresses its expression. The reported switch is content-mediated, graded, and localized by activation patching to middle-layer representations associated with observational rows—going beyond the standard assumption that the pretraining mixture alone determines causal reasoning.

Main result: With the same training recipe, purely observational context caused sign reversal in 29/50 synthetic worlds, mixed context in 19/50, and aligned interventional probes produced the correct sign in 41/50. Removing observational evidence yielded ratio_true=+0.56. Strong reversals persisted across 11/11 matched cases on a second seed; at 0.93B parameters, reversal rates were 31.8% versus 6% in the probe-only arm. Evidence averaging reduced sign errors from 26% to 9%.

Limitation: Evidence is confined mainly to controlled synthetic worlds, one reported 0.93B-scale robustness test, and an abstract-level CLadder audit. The abstract does not report comparisons across model families, larger scales, statistical confidence intervals, public code or data, or broad real-world causal-reasoning validation. Activation patching provides localization evidence but does not by itself establish a complete causal mechanism.

Relevance: The paper directly matches the query “causal reasoning” and addresses when language models use interventional evidence, why observational context can override learned causal direction, and how causal evaluations can reduce probe-sampling errors.

Tags: causal reasoning, causality, interventional data, Simpson's paradox, language models, in-context evidence, activation patching, CLadder

Figure note: A useful image would be the paper’s framework or causal pipeline figure showing how observational versus interventional evidence enters the inference context, suppresses or activates the learned causal response, and maps onto the localized middle-layer observational rows.

item.title: TRACT: Temporally Routed Action Chunks with Chronological Phase Authority for Contact-Rich Manipulation
item.description:
Priority: 49/100 (TL;DR only, confidence: high)

Quality dimensions: Author 26, Paper 57, Empirical 68, Reproducibility 25, Manuscript 75

Missing quality signals: Author affiliations and institutional metadata, Author citation counts and h-indexes, DOI, journal, or conference acceptance, Citation and influential-citation information, Open-source code or repository, Public dataset or demonstration logs

Score evidence: The work is an arXiv v1 manuscript in cs.RO with 6 pages and 3 figures.; Evaluation covers six real-robot variants with ten trials each.; Full TRACT reports 10/10 success, 99.00% median wipe completion, zero phase ambiguity, and zero stalls.; Component-related comparisons report ambiguity falling from 8/10 to 0/10 and stalls from 4/10 to 0/10.

TL;DR: TRACT improves phase-structured action chunking for contact-rich robot manipulation by explicitly routing future actions across a single procedural phase boundary and compensating for suppressed physical responses.

Problem: Conventional phase conditioning assigns the robot's current phase to an entire predicted action chunk, creating a temporal mismatch when that chunk crosses into the next procedural phase; contact resistance can additionally cause execution stalls.

Method: TRACT factorizes each chunk into an accepted current phase and one CURRENT-to-NEXT boundary. A task-local graph enforces chronological phase transitions, a cumulative boundary distribution monotonically routes future queries through phase-specific query and action paths, and a causal response-deficit integrator adds arm compensation when intended motion does not produce an eligible subsequent response.

Key contribution: The main novelty is phase-aware routing inside an action chunk rather than labeling the whole chunk with its initial phase, combined with explicit chronological authority and response-deficit integration for contact execution. The abstract presents this as a structurally monotonic treatment of procedural boundaries, although the package-level comparison does not isolate routing from other implementation differences.

Main result: Across six real-robot variants with ten trials each, full TRACT reports 10/10 full-sequence success, 99.00% median wipe completion with an 88.75–100.00% range, zero observed phase ambiguity, and zero stalls. In a package comparison, the routed method achieved 6/10 successes and 77.08% median completion versus 3/10 and 8.03% for the flat package. Chronological authority reduced ambiguity from 8/10 to 0/10, while response integration reduced stalls from 4/10 to 0/10.

Limitation: The package comparison is explicitly confounded by generator-package differences and therefore does not isolate the effect of temporal routing. The abstract also supplies only ten trials per variant and gives no statistical significance tests, broader task or robot coverage, standard-baseline comparison, code, public data, or independent reproduction evidence.

Relevance: The paper matches “causality” primarily through its causal response-deficit integrator, where policy intent is compared with subsequent physical response. It is relevant to causal feedback in robot control, but appears only indirectly relevant if the query targets causal inference, causal discovery, or counterfactual reasoning.

Tags: robot imitation learning, action chunking, contact-rich manipulation, phase conditioning, temporal routing, causal feedback, real-robot evaluation

Figure note: A useful image would be the paper's architecture figure showing the task-local phase graph, the cumulative CURRENT-to-NEXT boundary distribution, phase-specific query/action routing, and the response-deficit feedback loop.

TL;DR: A real-time event-camera framework enables upper-body humanoid teleoperation with 23–34 ms photon-to-action latency and improved tracking over RGB baselines in fast-motion, backlit, and sub-5-lux conditions.

Problem: The paper studies real-time human-to-humanoid upper-body motion imitation when conventional frame-based RGB sensing becomes unreliable because of rapid motion, severe backlighting, or very low illumination.

item.title: FairFund-Bench: Evaluating Distributive Bias in LLM Resource Allocation
item.description:
Priority: 69/100 (Skim, confidence: high)

Quality dimensions: Author 40, Paper 65, Empirical 83, Reproducibility 85, Manuscript 88

Missing quality signals: Author affiliation and institution, Author citation count and h-index, DOI, journal, or conference acceptance, Paper citation and influential-citation information, Statistical significance or confidence intervals, Exact effect sizes and complete metric values

Score evidence: The benchmark contains 600 requests calibrated against 1.3 million real GoFundMe campaigns.; Experiments cover 14 models, three domains, four race categories, two gender categories, and five causal framings.; Audit task, comparison context, and transparency are varied systematically.; The abstract reports direction-changing demographic effects and causal-framing effects roughly ten times larger.

TL;DR: FairFund-Bench shows that measured demographic bias in LLM resource allocation can reverse direction depending on audit design, while welfare-deservingness framings exert much larger and more consistent effects.

Problem: The paper studies why audits of demographic discrimination in LLM-assisted allocation of scarce resources produce inconsistent findings, particularly across race and gender groups.

Method: It introduces FairFund-Bench, containing 600 financial-assistance requests generated from human-authored templates calibrated against 1.3 million GoFundMe campaigns. The benchmark varies evaluation task (rating, ranking, or allocation), comparison context (single or multiple stimuli), audit transparency, three assistance domains, four race categories, two gender categories, and five causal framings of need. Fourteen models are scored on demographic bias, deservingness alignment, cross-task consistency, and cross-context consistency.

Key contribution: The genuinely new contribution is a controlled benchmark that treats audit format itself as an experimental variable, demonstrating that apparently contradictory bias findings can be artifacts of task, context, and transparency. It also separates demographic effects from causal narratives about deservingness.

Main result: Across 14 models, minorities tend to be advantaged in individual ratings but some groups are penalized in side-by-side rankings. Demographic bias is small overall but several times larger in disguised than transparent audits; causal framing effects are approximately an order of magnitude larger and remain consistent across models and formats.

Limitation: The abstract does not report uncertainty estimates, statistical significance, effect-size values, per-model results, robustness checks, or comparisons with alternative audit benchmarks. The requests are template-based and centered on financial assistance, so external validity beyond this domain remains unestablished.

Relevance: The paper matches the causality query through its controlled manipulation of five causal framings of need and its finding that these framings strongly affect allocations. However, it is primarily an LLM fairness and audit-methodology paper rather than a contribution to causal inference or causal discovery.

item.title: Doubly Robust Functional Representation Learning for Longitudinal Causal Inference with Irregular Histories

TL;DR: DR-FRL learns estimand-targeted representations of irregular longitudinal functional histories so doubly robust causal estimators can retain efficient-influence-function guarantees beyond scalar history summaries.

Problem: Longitudinal causal data often contain laboratory measurements, physiological signals, sensor streams, or image-derived features observed at unequal and informative times; conventional doubly robust estimators generally require scalar summaries, while ordinary sequence representations are optimized for prediction rather than valid causal estimating equations.

Method: The paper proposes Doubly Robust Functional Representation Learning (DR-FRL), a cross-fitted workflow combining functional and temporal encoders with outcome, treatment, and censoring nuisance heads. It selects and evaluates learned states using efficient-influence-function-targeted validation plus calibration, overlap, tail, and ablation diagnostics. Under stated information-preservation, rate, overlap, calibration, and stability assumptions, representation error contributes through the same second-order product remainder as nuisance-estimation error.

Key contribution: The main novelty is tying representation learning for irregular functional histories directly to the target causal estimand and its efficient influence function, rather than relying on scalar summaries or prediction-trained sequence embeddings. The paper also distinguishes Catoni aggregation as a bounded-influence point estimator rather than presenting it as a substitute for Wald inference.

Main result: Simulations reportedly show gains under high-dimensional functional confounding, informative measurement, weak support, and heavy-tailed pseudo-outcomes. A VitalDB audit finds that DR-FRL can process irregular laboratory point clouds but yields a useful negative result: scalar laboratory summaries already contain much of the endpoint-relevant information for the studied ICU-disposition endpoint. The abstract provides no numerical effect sizes or uncertainty estimates.

Limitation: Evidence is limited in the abstract to simulations and one VitalDB audit, without numerical results, named baselines, statistical uncertainty, or robustness details. The theoretical guarantee depends on the learned state preserving the nuisance information required by the efficient influence function, which may be difficult to verify empirically. No code, affiliations, publication venue, DOI, or explicit data-release information is supplied.

Relevance: This paper directly matches the causal inference query and is especially relevant to researchers studying longitudinal causal estimation, doubly robust methods, representation learning, irregularly sampled clinical histories, informative observation times, and efficient-influence-function-based inference.

item.title: The Role of Causality in Algorithmic Recourse
item.description:
Priority: 50/100 (Skim, confidence: medium)

Quality dimensions: Author 26, Paper 58, Empirical 64, Reproducibility 25, Manuscript 82

Missing quality signals: author affiliations and institution quality, author citation counts and h-indexes, conference or journal acceptance, DOI, paper citation and influential-citation data, open-source code or repository

Score evidence: The work uses a structural causal model to represent feature interactions and effects on the true label.; The authors state that causal responses make the optimization non-convex even with standard convex losses.; The abstract claims existence and efficient-computation conditions for performatively stable solutions.; Experiments cover semi-synthetic and real credit datasets and compare against standard empirical risk minimization.

TL;DR: The paper develops a causal performative framework for algorithmic recourse that accounts for how recommended actions alter features, true qualifications, and future model behavior, aiming to produce stable policies that discourage classifier gaming.

Problem: Standard algorithmic-recourse methods optimize for changing a classifier’s prediction but may recommend actions that do not improve the individual’s true qualifications, induce strategic gaming and distribution shift, reduce predictive accuracy, and become ineffective after retraining.

Method: The authors model recourse actions and behavioral responses using a structural causal model within a performative-prediction framework. They formulate the resulting non-convex optimization problem, characterize conditions for the existence of performatively stable solutions, and propose simple iterative dynamics that can efficiently compute such solutions under those conditions.

Key contribution: The central novelty is connecting causal recourse with performative stability: the framework explicitly tracks how actions propagate among features and affect the true label, rather than treating prediction flipping as the sole objective. It also supplies theoretical existence and computation conditions for stable equilibria under strategic behavioral responses.

Main result: According to the abstract, experiments on semi-synthetic and real credit datasets consistently outperform standard empirical risk minimization and reduce the need for repeated retraining under agent-induced distribution shifts. No numerical effect sizes, uncertainty estimates, or detailed baseline comparisons are provided.

TL;DR: The paper uses causal reasoning and adversarial representation probing to determine whether clinical covariates provide useful disease signal or harmful shortcut information in prostate MRI cancer grading.

Problem: Deep prostate MRI grading models may encode clinical covariates, but it is unclear whether these dependencies reflect tumour pathology, non-generalising shortcuts, or irrelevant information.

Method: The authors model MRI appearance and ISUP grade as observations of latent tumour pathology, then adversarially suppress the decodability of one clinical covariate at a time while preserving grade prediction; changes in predictive performance are used to characterize each covariate as a nuisance correlate, disease-related proxy, or irrelevant variable.

Key contribution: The main novelty is a representation-level causal probing framework that combines a latent-pathology causal interpretation with targeted adversarial suppression, allowing covariate dependence to be evaluated empirically rather than merely assumed.

Main result: On 2,903 prostate MRI examinations with external validation on 576 patients, suppressing age, BMI, and alcohol use improved binary ISUP Grade Group >=2 AUC by 1.23%, 0.84%, and 1.42%, respectively (all p<0.05), whereas suppressing PSA and prostate volume reduced AUC by 1.91% and 7.61% (all p<0.001).

Limitation: The abstract does not establish causal effects through intervention, report comparison baselines, or test joint suppression of correlated covariates. It also omits cohort characteristics, subgroup robustness, implementation details, and evidence that the identified dependencies generalize beyond the reported external dataset.

Relevance: This is a strong match for the query "causal reasoning": it explicitly introduces a causal interpretation of latent pathology, imaging, labels, and clinical covariates, then operationalizes that reasoning through adversarial probing. Its claims concern diagnosing learned dependence rather than full causal identification.
